The email you keep not sending: first lines and follow-ups
The email you keep not sending: first lines and follow-ups
An email that doesn't say what it wants gets answered slowly. Decide three things, write the first line, and know how to chase when no one replies.
7 min read
Updated 26 September 2026
In this guide
10
sections
Write one line saying what needs to happen because of this email, put it in the first three lines, read the draft once against a short check, and send it. If no one answers, wait a set number of days, then chase by a different route and ask for a date, not an update.
This is for the email that's been sitting in your drafts, or in your head, for days: a landlord, a school, a company, a relative. It can't tell you what to say about anything legal or medical, and it isn't advice on how you should feel about an email. It's practical help with the first line and the follow-up.
Example days; shorten them if a deadline is close.
You know who it's to. You know roughly what it's about. What's missing is a way to begin, so you open a blank message, write "Hi,", and close it again. The draft grows a paragraph of background, then an apology, then a second apology, and by then it's a bigger job than the one you started with.
A blank draft is the whole problem, so don't start blank
Example: an email that's been avoided for a week
An illustration, not a real account. Say your boiler has been making a noise for two weeks and you need the letting agent to send someone. Here is what goes on the page before you write a word of the email.
What it's for
What's on the page
Asking for something.
Who it's to
What's on the page
The letting agent, Riverside Lettings.
What needs to happen
What's on the page
Someone comes to look at the boiler this week.
First line
What's on the page
Hello, I'm hoping you can help me with something. The boiler in flat 3 has been making a loud noise for two weeks and I'd like someone to come and look at it.
Subject line
What's on the page
Boiler noise in flat 3: can someone visit this week?
The decision
What's on the page

First line
Hello, I'm hoping you can help me with something. The boiler in flat 3 has been making a loud noise for two weeks and I'd like someone to come and look at it.
Subject line
Boiler noise in flat 3: can someone visit this week?
How to write it
Say what the email is for: asking, replying, saying no, chasing, or explaining a problem. If it's two of those, it's two emails.
Say who it's to, by name if you have one. It stops you writing to a crowd.
Write what needs to happen because of it, in one line, with a date if there is one. An email that doesn't say what it wants is answered slowly, or not at all.
Write your first line from the list below. Change it, or write your own. The rest is usually easier once this exists.
Add only what they need to act: the dates, the reference number, the one thing you already tried. Leave the history for later if they ask.
Write a subject line that says the ask, not just the topic.
A first line to start from
Pick the closest. Getting this one sentence down is most of the work.
Pick the one you are facing
Asking
Replying
Saying no
Chasing
Explaining a problem
“
Hello, I'm hoping you can help me with something.
”
“
Hello, thank you for getting back to me. To answer your question:
”
“
Hello, thank you for asking me. I'm not going to be able to do it this time.
”
“
Hello, I got in touch about this a little while ago and I haven't heard back yet. Could you let me know where it stands?
”
“
Hello, I'm having a problem and I'd like to explain what's happened so it can be sorted out.
”
Subject lines that get opened
Say the ask in the subject. Vague ones are easy to leave for later.
Question
Try
Question about my March invoice: can you confirm the amount?
Following up
Try
Reply needed by Friday: lease renewal form
Problem
Try
Boiler noise in flat 3: can someone visit this week?
Hi
Try
Can't host in March: telling you now so you have time
Instead of
Try
Question
Question about my March invoice: can you confirm the amount?

Hi

Before you send it
Read it once against these, then send it. Reading it a fourth time doesn't make it better.
6 things to do
What you want is in the first three lines.
The date, if there is one, is in there.
Anything you meant to attach is attached.
It's short enough to read on a phone.
What you were told before is in there, if you're chasing or explaining a problem.
You've apologized no more than once, if you're saying no or chasing.
Ticks are for this visit only. Nothing here is saved anywhere.
The moment you press send, the job changes from writing to waiting, and waiting needs its own plan. Without one, the email drops out of your head and you find out three weeks later that nothing happened.
When no one replies
A chase plan (example)
The days are a suggestion we'd use for something that isn't an emergency. Shorten them if a deadline is close. Write the check-back date down the day you send.
Day 0: you send
Note the date, who it went to, and what you asked for.
Day 5: nothing yet
Chase by a different route, such as a call if you emailed. Ask for a date.
Day 10: still nothing
Write again to the same person and add a second person or a general address.
Day 15: still nothing
Decide whether it needs escalating, or whether you can let it go.
Chase lines, by what you're waiting on
Ask for a date rather than an update, because an update can be nothing. A date is something you can hold them to.
Pick the one you are facing
A reply
A decision
Money owed to you
Something being fixed
A document or form
“
Hello, I got in touch a little while ago about this and I haven't heard back. Could you tell me where it stands?
”
“
Hello, I'm following up because I need to know either way. When do you think you'll be able to tell me?
”
“
Hello, I'm following up because it's still outstanding. Can you tell me when it will be dealt with?
”
“
Hello, I'm checking in because it hasn't been sorted yet. Can you tell me what's happening and when?
”
“
Hello, I'm still waiting on this. Could you tell me when I can expect it, or what you need from me first?
”
Chasing by the same route that already went unanswered is usually the slower option. If you emailed, try a phone call, or the other way around.

has an opening for chasing.
What can go wrong
You keep editing. If you've changed the first line four times, send the fourth one. A slightly plain email you sent beats a polished one that's still in drafts.
You write everything at once. If the email is more than about ten lines, cut the background and offer to send it on request.
You chase too soon and feel rude. Waiting until your check-back date is the fix, so the date decides, not the feeling.
You chase in the same channel, again. A second unread email tends to get the same result as the first.
The email is really a refusal or bad news. For those, a call may be kinder.
How to say no or give bad news on the phone
covers it.
Questions people ask
How do I start an email I keep putting off?
Start with one line saying what you want, not with a greeting and background. Pick a first line that fits: asking, replying, saying no, chasing, or explaining a problem. Once that sentence exists the rest tends to follow. If you're stuck, write only the first line and save the draft. That counts as a start.
How long should I wait before following up on an email?
There's no fixed rule. For something that isn't urgent, many people wait somewhere around a week. If a deadline is close, wait two or three days. Whatever you choose, write the date down when you send, so the check-back is a plan, not a feeling.
How do I follow up politely when no one replied?
Keep it short and specific. Say when you last got in touch, then ask for a date rather than an update: "Could you let me know when I can expect this?" Avoid apologizing more than once. If the first message went by email, try a call this time.
Why do I dread replying to emails?
Emails can feel like open-ended obligations, and a first line is the hardest part to produce. Some people also find it uncomfortable to disappoint or ask. If dread of messages is getting in the way of work or health, a clinician is the right person to talk to. Practically, a fixed first line and a short check make the task smaller.
What if I still get no reply?
Change the route, then the person. Try a phone call, or write to a second contact or a general address, and mention that you've written before. Note each attempt with the date. If it involves money or a deadline, ask for a named person and a date.
Where the Companion fits
The Send the email walkthrough in
ADHD Life Companion
asks what the email is for, who it's to, and what needs to happen because of it, then offers a first line you can use or replace with your own and lists the checks to read before you send. A Follow something up walkthrough asks how you last got in touch and what you need from them now. When you say you're waiting on someone, it keeps the item as Waiting with a check-back date ten days out, and lets you keep a note of who. It doesn't send email or read your inbox, and it isn't a treatment or medical advice.
This is general information written to help you get organized, not professional advice.
